topic.title: Why Time Feels Faster Every Year

copy.title: STOP LETTING THE YEARS BLUR

steps.why: sameness is the signal your brain has stopped recording new information.

steps.rule: Name one thing that felt new today
steps.why: a labelled novelty gets stored as a distinct memory, not folded into the blur.

steps.rule: Schedule one unfamiliar thing this week
steps.why: a new route, a new task, a new conversation stretches the perceived length of that week.

steps.rule: Review what you did differently this month
steps.why: the review forces your brain to count distinct events instead of averaging them into one.

steps.rule: Raise the unfamiliarity target each quarter
steps.why: without a rising threshold, the brain re-categorises last month's novelty as routine and compresses it.

copy.kicker: New inputs make the clock slow down.
copy.thumb_scene: Wick stands upright on a plain white studio background, holding a blank wall calendar in one hand and a single bright sticky note in the other, looking directly into the camera with a still, unhurried expression, nothing else in frame.
copy.send_to: the friend who said this year went by in a blink

caption:
Most people think a busy year means a long year.

It doesn't.

Busyness on repeat is the fastest way to make five years vanish into one.

The hidden rule is this: your brain only stores what surprises it, so a life built on Systems that repeat without variation quietly switches off the Mind's recording function.

A year of identical Tuesdays gets filed as one Tuesday. That is the cost. Not just time that felt short. Time you genuinely cannot account for when someone asks what changed.

Count the distinct things you did last month.

What number did you land on, and does it surprise you?

Light one. Pass it on. 🕯️
